title: Near Mint Conditions
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien offers a contrarian take on teacher working conditions in Victoria, Australia, arguing that ongoing employment security, annual incremental pay increases, and high workforce demand place Victorian teachers in an enviable position compared to most professions. He contends that the erosion of structured professional development (replacing the PDP process with a low-accountability 'Statement of Expectation') removes incentives for teachers to improve, risking complacency analogous to subsidised industries that fail to compete when protections are removed. A key claim is that workload problems are more often self-imposed at the school and individual level—through bespoke resource creation, excessive lesson planning, and continuous reporting—than imposed by systemic agreements. Better outcomes would come from school leaders centralising tasks, using shared quality resources, and removing low-impact activities. Brien argues the education system also fails to reward exceptional teaching in the classroom, driving high performers toward administration or away to independent schools.
points: Victorian teachers have unprecedented job security, annual pay increments, and high demand—yet union negotiations focus on 'better conditions' that often shift rather than reduce workload.

The replacement of structured PDP (Professional Development Plans) with a 'Statement of Expectation' effectively eliminates incentive structures: teachers progress through salary increments simply by attending a conversation without real accountability for outcomes.
The parallel to Australia's subsidised automotive industry is sharp: remove incentives to improve, and complacency follows; when protections eventually lift, the capacity to compete is gone.

Most workload complaints stem from school-level or individual choices—bespoke resource creation, micro-managed lesson plans, continuous reporting—all of which can be addressed by leadership centralising tasks and adopting shared, high-quality resources.

A great teacher can add 18 months to a student's learning progress, yet the system provides no differential reward for excellence in the classroom, pushing top performers into administration or independent schools.
quotes: In a time where jobs are being replaced by AI, whole industries are crumbling and entry level opportunities are ceasing to exist, teaching remains in demand.
If there is no incentive to improve, improvement is unlikely.
The conditions and workloads of teachers are more negatively impacted at a school and individual level than at a state level.

To solve the workload issues for so many of these areas would not occur in a new agreement for wages and conditions. They need to occur at a school level where leaders meaningfully take action to centralise activities, increase consistency and remove tasks with minimal impact on learning.
A great teacher can add months to a students learning progress, while an ineffective teacher can send a student only minimally forward

workload is no where near as bad as it is advertised to be. So much of it is created at a personal and school level that can only be solved by ourselves and leadership teams and a new agreement is barely going to scratch the surface.
